answers.answer: Close to nothing. BM25 scores by token matching between two high-dimensional sparse vectors with TF-IDF weights, so the only components that contribute are tokens present on both sides. Different vocabulary for the same idea means the vectors overlap nowhere that carries weight, and the passage is not retrieved however well it answers the question.
accept: states the score is zero or near zero
attributes it to matching on shared tokens rather than on meaning
connects that to the sparse vector representation with per-token weights

answers.answer: The embeddings for the whole corpus. Because the passage encoder never sees the query, a passage's vector depends only on the passage, so every passage can be encoded and indexed ahead of time. At query time the system embeds the query and ranks passages by closeness in that space.
accept: says passage or corpus embeddings can be computed in advance and indexed
explains that a passage vector depends only on the passage because the encoders run independently
says query time work is embedding the query and comparing it against the stored vectors

answers.answer: The in-batch negatives are the passages already in the batch that belong to the other questions, so they cost no extra retrieval. The one additional negative per question is supplied by BM25, which puts the lexical ranker inside the dense retriever's training loop.
accept: says the negatives are the other questions' passages in the same batch
notes that they are reused from the batch rather than fetched separately
says the extra negative per question comes from BM25

answers.answer: Whether the retriever was trained on the distribution it is being asked about. DPR's numbers are in-domain, with training data from the datasets it is evaluated on; BEIR measures zero-shot transfer to 18 datasets across tasks and domains, and reports that in-domain performance is not a good indicator for out-of-domain generalization. On BEIR, DPR, the only evaluated system not trained on MS MARCO, generalized the worst of the systems tested.
accept: names the in-domain versus zero-shot or out-of-domain distinction as the condition
states that in-domain results do not predict out-of-domain generalization
reports that DPR generalized worst on the BEIR benchmark

answers.answer: The authors conjecture that the annotators wrote their questions after reading the passage, which leaves a high lexical overlap between questions and passages and gives BM25 an advantage, and that the data came from only about 500 Wikipedia articles, which makes the training distribution extremely biased. Both are properties of the collection procedure rather than of the retrieval task, so the win is an artefact of how the dataset was annotated.
accept: says annotators wrote questions while looking at the passage, producing high lexical overlap that favours BM25
identifies that as a property of how the data was collected rather than of the task
credits it as the authors' conjecture rather than a measured cause, or mentions the small pool of source articles biasing the training distribution

answers.answer: BEIR supports the lexical leg: BM25 remains a strong baseline for zero-shot retrieval, and dense models that are strong on some datasets fall significantly behind it on others, which is the situation you are in with no labelled queries. DPR supports the dense leg where in-domain data does exist, and reports that combining DPR with BM25 improves results further in some cases, in both the single- and multi-dataset settings. The limit is in the words 'in some cases': the paper does not claim the combination helps everywhere.
accept: cites BM25 as a strong zero-shot baseline as the reason to keep the lexical ranker
cites dense retrieval's in-domain strength or uneven per-dataset results as the reason to keep the dense ranker
states that the reported gain from combining the two holds in some cases rather than universally
